::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The brief

You work as a data scientist at an energy company. You have the hourly electricity generation of its
portfolio, with the weather, up to midnight on 27 October 2026. The grid operator wants a forecast for
the next 48 hours, hour by hour, with a 95% prediction interval: the interval tells them how much reserve
to hold.

Everyone in the group forecasts the same data. Session 1 gives you 80 minutes. After that you have two
days at home, and you may use any method you like.
:::

## The data

Three files on Moodle:

- `train.csv`: the history, about 3.8 years of hours, with the target `y` and the actual weather.
- `weather_forecast.csv`: a weather forecast for the 48 hours you predict.
- `_project.ipynb`: the template. To open it in Colab, use *File → Upload notebook*. When you run it, it
  asks you to upload the two CSV files.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ds` | the hour |
| `y` | electricity generated in that hour; this is what you forecast |
| `cloud_cover` | from 0 (clear) to 1 (overcast), in steps of 0.25 |
| `temperature` | °C |
| `wind_speed` | m/s |
| `pressure` | mm Hg |
| `humidity` | % |
| `daylight` | 1 while the sun is above the horizon |
| `air_density` | kg/m³ |

::: {.callout-note}
## The weather for the horizon is a forecast

`weather_forecast.csv` is what a weather service would have issued for those 48 hours. It is close to the
weather that followed, but it has errors, and they grow from the first day to the second. You may use it
or leave it out. Say which you did in the report, and why.
:::

The template loads the data, defines the three metrics, scores the benchmark on a validation window, and
writes and checks the submission file. There is no model in it. The submission cell starts from the
benchmark, so if you run the notebook from top to bottom you have a valid file within five minutes. The
rest of the session is for beating it.

## The task

Forecast the 48 hours that follow the last hour of `train.csv`. For every hour, give a point forecast
and a 95% prediction interval. You can use any method or library, from the course or outside it.

### The submission file

The file is called `SURNAME_project.csv` and has 48 rows and four columns, in this order:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| `ds` | the hour as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`, the same hours as in `weather_forecast.csv` |
| `forecast` | the point forecast |
| `lower_95` | the lower bound of the 95% interval, 0 or above |
| `upper_95` | the upper bound |

`check_submission` in the template tests all of this. We cannot score a file that fails it.

## Scoring

Each forecast gets three scores on the 48 hidden hours. Lower is better for all three.

$$
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{48}\sum_{t}(y_t - \hat y_t)^2}
\qquad
\text{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{48}\sum_{t}\left|\frac{y_t - \hat y_t}{y_t}\right|
$$

$$
\text{Winkler} = \frac{1}{48}\sum_t \Big[(U_t - L_t) + \tfrac{2}{\alpha}(L_t - y_t)_+ + \tfrac{2}{\alpha}(y_t - U_t)_+\Big],
\qquad \alpha = 0.05
$$

The Winkler score adds the width of the interval to a penalty for every hour the actual value falls
outside it. The penalty is 40 times the distance to the nearest bound, so a narrow interval that misses
can cost more than a wide one.

The benchmark is a seasonal naive forecast with a daily season. Each hour of the next two days gets the
value of the same hour on the last day of `train.csv`, and the interval is the standard one for seasonal
naive. The template computes it for you. On the leaderboard it is listed as `----SNAIVE----`.

### Public and private leaderboards

The 48 hidden hours are split in two, as in a Kaggle competition. The first 24 hours make up the public
part. On Wednesday and Thursday at 09:00 we score the latest file each of you has submitted on these
hours and publish the table. The last 24 hours make up the private part, which stays hidden until
Session 2, and the final ranking uses only these hours.

The split protects you from tuning your model to the leaderboard. If you could see your score on all 48
hours, every resubmission would teach your model something about the answer. The public table shows
roughly where you stand, and the ranking is decided on hours nobody has seen.

The ranking on the private 24 hours combines the three metrics:

$$
\text{rank} = 0.3 \cdot \text{rank}_{\text{RMSE}} + 0.3 \cdot \text{rank}_{\text{MAPE}} + 0.4 \cdot \text{rank}_{\text{Winkler}}
$$

We rank the better of your two submissions, the Session 1 file or the final one. If a change you made at
home turns out worse on the private hours, you lose nothing. This rule replaces the condition in the
syllabus that the final result must be no worse than the Session 1 result.

## Points

| Criterion | Points | Based on |
|---|---:|---|
| Valid Session 1 submission: correct format, in by 11:30 | 5 | Session 1 |
| Beating the benchmark in Session 1 | 8 | Session 1 |
| Final accuracy, ranked against the group | 5 | final submission |
| Methodology and diagnostics | 8 | report |
| Code quality and reproducibility | 2 | repository |
| Defence and presentation | 4 | Session 2 |
| Total | 32 | |

### Beating the benchmark (8 points)

We compare your Session 1 file with the benchmark on all 48 hidden hours:

$$
\text{skill} = \frac{\text{RMSE of your forecast}}{\text{RMSE of the benchmark}}
$$

| Skill | Points |
|---|---:|
| below 1 (you beat the benchmark) | 8 |
| above 1, up to 1.1 (within 10% of it) | 5 |
| exactly 1 (the template's benchmark unchanged), or above 1.1 | 2 |

### Final accuracy (5 points)

We take the better of your two submissions on the private 24 hours. A submission beats the benchmark
there if it has a lower RMSE or a better combined rank than `----SNAIVE----`; either one is enough.
Everyone who beats the benchmark is ranked with the formula above. The top third of that list gets 5
points, the middle third 4 and the bottom third 3. A submission that does not beat the benchmark gets
1 point.

If only one of your two files beats the benchmark, that is the file we rank.

### Methodology and diagnostics (8 points)

You decide which analyses to run. The report should answer four questions, worth 2 points each.

| Question | What to cover |
|---|---|
| What is in the series? | The patterns you found, how the series changes over time, how the weather relates to it, and how all of that shaped your model. |
| How did you check the forecast before submitting it? | How you compared your forecast with the benchmark on data you held back: which windows, how many, and what they showed. |
| How good is your interval? | How you built the 95% interval and how you checked it on held-back data, with coverage and the Winkler score. |
| What is left, and what did not work? | The residuals of your final model, and the approaches you tried and dropped, with the reasons. |

::: {.callout-important}
## How the report is marked

Points follow the reasoning. A model that lost to the benchmark can earn the full 8 if you read the
numbers correctly and your conclusion follows from them. An approach that failed is worth reporting: it
tells us what you tried and what you learned. If you go beyond the obvious steps and can explain why,
that counts in your favour.
:::

### Code quality and reproducibility (2 points)

One point if the repository runs from a clean start and produces your final file. One point for a
`README` that explains how to run it and, if you used LLMs, how you used them.

### Defence and presentation (4 points)

Two points for the talk, which should show how you approached the problem and how your forecast did
against the benchmark. Two points for your answers to two or three questions about the project and about decisions you made in
your labs.

## Between the sessions

You can keep improving your forecast at home with any model, library or amount of tuning. LLMs are
allowed; describe how you used them in the `README`.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two rules

- Use only the data you were given. The series has been disguised. Searching for its original source
  counts as looking up the answer, and we treat it as cheating.
- Do your own work. You are welcome to discuss methods with each other, and Session 2 is where everyone
  compares approaches. Do not share forecasts or files.
:::

## Final submission: Thursday 5 November, 23:59

Upload to the *Final* activity on Moodle:

1. `SURNAME_project.csv` with your improved forecast, in the same format. If nothing you tried beat your
   Session 1 forecast, submit that file again and explain why in the report.
2. A link to a public GitHub repository that contains:
   - the notebook or scripts that produce the file from `train.csv` and `weather_forecast.csv` (put both
     data files in the repository);
   - the report, as a Jupyter notebook or a PDF, in English or Ukrainian;
   - a `README` with instructions for running the code and a note on LLM use.
3. Your slides as a PDF, made with any tool.

## Session 2: Friday 6 November

Each of you has five minutes, followed by two or three questions. Show the main points: your approach,
your results against the benchmark, and what you would do differently. After the talks we open the
private leaderboard and compare how everyone approached the same data.

## If something goes wrong

- If an air raid or a power or connection outage interrupts you during Session 1, your deadline moves by
  the time you lost. Tell the instructor the same day. If the whole group loses more than 20 minutes, the
  session is rescheduled for everyone. The hidden hours and the leaderboard stay unpublished until every
  Session 1 file is in.
- If you cannot present on Friday, you present online at an extra slot within a week. The questions and
  the criteria are the same.
